a(n) = (product of digits of n; n in binary notation) mod 2. This sequence is a transformation of the Thue-Morse sequence (A010060), since there exists a function f such that f(sum of digits of n) = (product of digits of n).

1 if n=0, floor(log_2(n+1)) - floor(log_2(n)) otherwise. G.f.: (1/x) * Sum_{k>=0} x^(2^k) = Sum_{k>=0} x^(2^k-1).

a(n) = 1 - A043545(n).

(PARI) {a(n) =( n++) == 2^valuation(n, 2)}; /* Michael Somos, Aug 25 2003 */

generic.title: Index to 2D 5-Neighbor Cellular Automata - OeisWiki
snippets:
## Introduction
**There are 1024 possible 2D 5-Neighbor Outer Totalistic Cellular Automata.** Wolfram's numbering scheme identifies these by rule numbers from 0 to 1023. See "A New Kind of Science" by Stephen Wolfram, pages 170-179 or the Eric Weisstein's "World of Mathematics" links below. The sequences in the OEIS generally represent a two-dimensional cellular automata (CA) on a square grid representing successive generations or stages.

generic.title: On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences
snippets:
## Conventions
The OEIS was limited to plain ASCII text until 2011, and it still uses a linear form of conventional mathematical notation (such as *f*(*n*) for functions, *n* for running variables, etc.). Greek letters are usually represented by their full names, *e.g.*, mu for μ, phi for φ. Every sequence is identified by the letter A followed by six digits, almost always referred to with leading zeros, *e.g.*, A000315 rather than A315.

### Lexicographical ordering
The OEIS maintains the lexicographical order of the sequences, so each sequence has a predecessor and a successor (its "context"). OEIS normalizes the sequences for lexicographical ordering, (usually) ignoring all initial zeros and ones, and also the sign of each element. Sequences of weight distribution codes often omit periodically recurring zeros.

### Entry fields
**ID number**: Every sequence in the OEIS has a serial number, a six-digit positive integer, prefixed by A (and zero-padded on the left prior to November 2004). The letter "A" stands for "absolute". Numbers are either assigned by the editor(s) or by an A number dispenser, which is handy for when contributors wish to send in multiple related sequences at once and be able to create cross-references.

generic.title: Federal Register :: Removing Deference to Prior USCIS Determinations of Eligibility
snippets:
### A. Purpose and Summary of the Proposed Regulatory Action
That regulation instructs USCIS officers to give deference to a prior determination of a petitioner's, applicant's, or beneficiary's eligibility when adjudicating a request filed on Form I-129, Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker, involving the same parties and the same underlying facts.^[1] This requirement most often applies when a petitioning employer seeks to extend a petition for an alien's employment or authorized stay in the United States under the same previously approved nonimmigrant worker classification.

This proposal would not prohibit USCIS officers from considering a prior approval where relevant. Rather, it would remove the requirement that officers begin from a position of deference to the prior approval. DHS believes that this change would better ensure that officers fully consider all relevant facts and evidence to ensure continued eligibility, and adjudicate each petition or request on a case-by-case basis to determine whether the petitioner has met its burden of proof to demonstrate continued eligibility for the benefit.

### E. Reliance Interests and Alternatives Considered
DHS recognizes that some U.S. employers and nonimmigrant workers may assert reliance interests in the continuation of the deference policy. For example, U.S. employers that expect the continued approval of their Form I-129 petitions may have made business arrangements based on an assumption that these nonimmigrant workers would be able to continue working for them.

This proposed change would not deprive U.S. employers of their ability to continue employing nonimmigrant workers, nor would it deprive nonimmigrant workers of their ability to continue working and living in the United States, so long as they are able to establish continued eligibility and obtain necessary approvals to continue such employment. Petitioners and beneficiaries do not have a legitimate expectation that an erroneous or unsupported prior approval would continue to result in future approvals.
